newsitem.title: USA: Collision looms for trade, biotech, consumer goals.
newsitem.headline: Collision looms for trade, biotech, consumer goals.

text.p: Bio-engineered versions of corn and soybeans -- two of the most widely planted U.S. crops -- will see a tumultuously sceptical reception if some consumer and environmental groups have their way.
The genetically altered varieties are being harvested for the first time this fall and would account for a tiny part of U.S. output.

Nonetheless, some European groups say they would forego all U.S. soybeans unless the new varieties are handled separately and labeled -- a costly demand for a product normally shipped and stored in huge, interchangable lots.

Activists who opposed bio-tinkering with U.S. milk and tomatoes planned to join the squabble on Monday, this time aiming at the biotech versions of corn and soybeans. News conferences were scheduled in Washington and Chicago.

"These (crops) are just about to be harvested, so we are launching our boycott at this point," said Ronnie Cummins of the Pure Food Campaign, which opposes biotech foods. The boycott would aim at a handful of well-known foods that are made with corn or soybean products.

If the dispute becomes heated enough, it could strain transatlantic trade relations. The European Union has approved marketing of one type of genetically engineered soybeans but has yet to decide whether to allow bio-corn on the market.
"It (corn) could become a trade issue," U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said last Tuesday.
Glickman said European objections to bio-soybeans were "worrisome" and reflected "what I call unsound science out there...shaping consumer attitudes."

U.S. officials say both products are safe and there was no reason to block them from sale or to require special labels because they are indistinguishable from other varieties. Like industry groups, U.S. officials say labeling is impractical considering the huge volume of U.S. corn and oilseeds.
Paul Drazek, Glickman's trade adviser, was to travel to Europe this week to discuss gene-altered corn and soybeans, among other topics.
The United States and the European Union have disagreed for several years over an EU ban on U.S. beef grown with the aid of synthetic growth hormones.
Opponents have had limited effect in the United States in trying to squash a tomato altered to stay fresh longer and a synthetic hormone that encourages cows to give more milk.

At issue in the dispute over soybeans is a variety adapted to be more tolerant of one herbicide, Roundup, made by Monsanto Co, St Louis. The corn has been altered to produce a bacterium that makes it resistance to the corn borer, a damaging pest.
A trade group, EuroCommerce, said last week that its members wanted to have the chance to meet consumer fears by putting labels on foods made with gene-altered soybeans.

"I think the farmers in the United States should be aware that almost 50 percent of their harvest is in danger, their (export) market is in danger and people might have the tendency to look for other products that do not contain soy," Heinrich Kroener said at a news conference.
The environmental group Greenpeace has campaigned against gene-altered corn and soybeans in Europe.
Corn and soybeans were planted on 144 million acres (56.7 million hectares) in the United States this year, an area equal to 225,000 square miles.
